changes.before: If the other confidence level becomes 0.90 instead of 0.99, is it wider than the 0.95 interval?
changes.after: A confidence interval is a range made from a sample. A 95% method is designed to cover the true mean about 95 times in 100 across repeated samples when its assumptions hold.

before: t.test(x)$conf.int gives a t-based interval for a population mean. Under its sampling/model assumptions, a 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed true mean in 95% of repeated samples; it is not a statement that 95% of individual future values lie in this realized interval.

For the same data and method, a higher confidence level produces a wider interval. The method depends on independent observations and a suitable mean-sampling model, especially with tiny samples. Synthetic numbers here demonstrate the computation, not scientific adequacy.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
x <- c(8, 9, 10, 11, 12)
base <- t.test(x, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
other <- t.test(x, conf.level = 0.99)$conf.int
width <- function(interval) interval[2] - interval[1]
cat(width(other) > width(base), "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: TRUE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Explain why this interval is not an individual prediction interval. You may trace it without a R interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A confidence interval is a range made from a sample. A 95% method is designed to cover the true mean about 95 times in 100 across repeated samples when its assumptions hold.
With the same sample and method, a 99% interval is wider than a 95% interval.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```r
x <- c(8, 9, 10, 11, 12)
base <- t.test(x, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
other <- t.test(x, conf.level = 0.99)$conf.int
width <- function(interval) interval[2] - interval[1]
cat(width(other) > width(base), "\n", sep = "")
```
The output is `TRUE`. The width comparison finds that the higher-confidence range is wider.

before.question: If the other confidence level becomes 0.90 instead of 0.99, is it wider than the 0.95 interval?
choices: It becomes an interval containing 90% of individual observations.
TRUE because all intervals have equal width.
FALSE; the lower-confidence interval is narrower.
before.explanation: Holding data and method fixed, the lower critical value for 90% confidence produces a narrower mean interval, not an individual prediction interval.

after.question: Is the 90% interval wider than the 95% interval here?
choices: They are always the same width.
after.explanation: The lower confidence level uses a smaller range for this sample.
